title: Hand Numbness and Tingling at Night: Is It Carpal Tunnel Syndrome?
metaDescription: Numb or tingling hands at night are often carpal tunnel syndrome. Learn the signs, simple treatments, when injection or surgery is considered, and red flags.
intro: Numb, tingling hands that wake you at night are often caused by carpal tunnel syndrome, though not always. It happens when a nerve at the wrist (the median nerve) is squeezed in a narrow passage called the carpal tunnel. It often eases with simple steps such as a night splint, and it sometimes settles by itself. An examination can confirm whether this is the cause.

sections.heading: What does carpal tunnel syndrome feel like?
sections.body: Most people notice numbness, tingling or pins and needles, mainly in the thumb, index, middle and ring fingers. Some have an ache in the hand or forearm, a weaker grip, or trouble with small tasks such as doing up buttons. You may drop things. It usually starts slowly, comes and goes at first, and then happens more often.

sections.heading: Why does my hand go numb at night?
sections.body: Symptoms are often worse at night and can wake you from sleep. Shaking the hand or letting it hang over the edge of the bed often brings relief. In the daytime, holding the wrist bent for a long time, for example on a phone or while driving, can bring it on. The tingling comes from pressure on the nerve.

sections.heading: What causes it, and who is more likely to get it?
sections.body: Swelling in the wrist, or a naturally narrow tunnel, squeezes the nerve. It is more common in women and older adults, in pregnancy, and in people with diabetes, arthritis or thyroid problems. Repeated wrist bending, hard gripping and a family history also raise the chance. Often several causes act together.

sections.heading: What is our usual approach to treatment?
sections.body: We start gently and move one step at a time, tailored to you.
bullets: Medicines first: paracetamol or ibuprofen may ease pain for a short time, although they do not treat the cause.
Night splint and activity changes: a splint keeps the wrist straight in bed. It can take up to 6 weeks to feel better. Cutting down on repeated wrist bending and hard gripping also helps.
Exercises: once pain eases, gentle hand and nerve-gliding exercises can be added. The evidence for them is small.
Physiotherapy machines such as ultrasound: we use these for pain relief only. A review of research rated the evidence for ultrasound as low quality, so the benefit is uncertain.

sections.heading: Does a steroid injection help?
sections.body: A steroid injection into the wrist reduces swelling around the nerve and helps in most cases. We offer it only to selected people, for pain relief, usually when a splint has not been enough. It does not last forever: the effect may wear off after weeks or months, and symptoms can return. Repeated injections may work less well or cause skin changes, so they are not always offered.

sections.heading: Do I need surgery?
sections.body: Not everyone does. Surgery is usually considered when symptoms are getting worse or have not settled with other treatments, or when numbness is constant or the thumb muscle has become thin. The surgeon cuts the tight ligament pressing on the nerve, usually as a day procedure under local anaesthetic (numbing medicine). Many people return to normal activities in about a month, but grip strength can take 2 to 3 months, and full recovery can take longer. Risks include infection, scarring and nerve injury. We explain the options, and you decide.

sections.heading: When should I see a doctor quickly?
sections.body: Get assessed promptly if numbness is constant, the muscle at the base of your thumb looks thinner, your grip is weak, or you keep dropping things. The same applies after a wrist injury, or if the wrist becomes red, hot or swollen, especially with fever. Early assessment matters because long-standing pressure on the nerve can sometimes lead to lasting numbness or weakness.

faqs.q: Can carpal tunnel syndrome go away on its own?
faqs.a: Sometimes. It can improve within a few months, particularly when it is linked to pregnancy. If it is getting worse or not going away, have it checked.

faqs.q: Does a wrist splint really help?
faqs.a: A splint worn at night keeps the wrist straight and is a common first step. It can take up to 6 weeks before you feel better.

faqs.q: Do I need a scan or nerve test?
faqs.a: Usually not. The diagnosis is normally made from your symptoms and an examination of your hand. Nerve tests or scans are used when the picture is unclear.
Usually yes, with changes. Cut down on repeated wrist bending and hard gripping, and adjust your workstation if needed.

faqs.q: Can pregnancy cause carpal tunnel syndrome?
faqs.a: Yes. Swelling during pregnancy can squeeze the nerve, and it often settles afterwards.
There is a small amount of evidence that they do. They are usually added once pain has eased.
